name: Computer Networks (Part 1)
details:
Computer Networks & Data Communications

Comprehensive knowledge map based on Sadi Sir's lectures covering Chapter 2 (Application Layer) and Lectures 7 to 14 (Transport Layer, Protocols, Flow/Congestion Control, and Security).

  • Scope: Application Layer & Transport Layer
  • Reference: Kurose & Ross (8e) + Forouzan (5e)
  • Total Slides: 366 slides

children.name: Chapter 2: Application Layer
children.details:
Application Layer Core

Principles of network applications, client-server vs P2P architectures, socket abstraction, transport layer service requirements (throughput, delay, loss sensitivity).

children.name: Principles of Network Apps
children.details:
Application Architectures

  • Client-Server: Dedicated server host, always-on, fixed IP; clients communicate through server (Web, Email).
  • P2P (Peer-to-Peer): Minimal/no dedicated servers; direct communication between peers; self-scalability (BitTorrent).
  • Socket Interface: API door between application process and transport layer.
  • Addressing: IP address (identifies host) + 16-bit Port number (identifies specific process).

children.name: Web & HTTP
children.details:
Hypertext Transfer Protocol (HTTP)

  • Port: 80 (HTTP), 443 (HTTPS) over TCP.
  • Stateless: Server maintains no info about past client requests.
  • HTTP/1.0 vs HTTP/1.1: Non-persistent (1 RTT per object) vs Persistent (multiple objects over 1 TCP connection, pipelining).
  • HTTP/2 & HTTP/3: Binary framing, multiplexing streams over single connection, HOL blocking solved in HTTP/3 via QUIC (UDP).
  • Cookies: Set-Cookie in server header, Cookie in client header for session state.
  • Caching & Conditional GET: If-modified-since returns 304 Not Modified if fresh.

children.name: Electronic Mail (SMTP/IMAP)
children.details:
Email Protocols

  • SMTP (RFC 5321): Push protocol, port 25, uses TCP to transfer mail between servers. 7-bit ASCII limitation (MIME extensions).
  • Mail Access Protocols: POP3 (authorization, download-and-delete or keep, stateless), IMAP (manipulate messages in folders on server, stateful), Webmail (HTTP).

children.name: Domain Name System (DNS)
children.details:
DNS Architecture

  • Role: Hostname to IP translation, host/mail server aliasing, load distribution.
  • Hierarchy: Root DNS servers -> Top-Level Domain (TLD: .com, .edu) -> Authoritative servers.
  • Queries: Iterative (local server queries hierarchy) vs Recursive (burden pushed to queried server).
  • Resource Records (RR): (Name, Value, Type, TTL). Type A (host->IP), Type NS (domain->authoritative server), Type CNAME (alias->canonical name), Type MX (mail server).

children.name: Video Streaming & CDNs
children.details:
Video Distribution

  • DASH: Dynamic Adaptive Streaming over HTTP. Server divides video into chunks encoded at multiple bitrates; client dynamically requests quality based on bandwidth.
  • CDNs: Content Distribution Networks. Enter Deep (servers close to users in access networks) vs Bring Home (fewer clusters at IXPs).

children.name: L7: Transport Layer Intro
children.details:
Transport Layer Role

Provides logical end-to-end communication between application processes on different hosts.

children.name: Transport vs Network Layer
children.details:
Scope Comparison

  • Network Layer: Logical communication between hosts (IP routing).
  • Transport Layer: Logical communication between processes (Port addressing).
  • Analogy: 12 kids writing letters in 2 houses (Network = postal service, Transport = Ann & Bill collecting and distributing letters to kids).

children.name: Multiplexing & Demux
children.details:
Ports & Demultiplexing

  • Multiplexing (Sender): Gathering data chunks from multiple sockets, adding transport headers, passing to network layer.
  • Demultiplexing (Receiver): Examining header fields to direct received segments to the correct socket.
  • Port Ranges (16 bits): 0-1023 (Well-known/System), 1024-49151 (Registered), 49152-65535 (Dynamic/Private/Ephemeral).
  • Connectionless Demux (UDP): Uses 2-tuple (dest IP, dest port).
  • Connection-Oriented Demux (TCP): Uses 4-tuple (src IP, src port, dest IP, dest port).

children.name: L8: Reliable Data Transfer (RDT)
children.details:
RDT Framework & Evolution

Building reliable transport over inherently unreliable underlying network layers.

children.name: RDT Protocol Evolution
children.details:
RDT Versions

  • rdt 1.0: Completely reliable underlying channel (no bit errors, no loss).
  • rdt 2.0: Channel with bit errors. Introduces Checksums, ACKs, and NAKs (Stop-and-Wait). Fatal flaw: what if ACK/NAK is corrupted?
  • rdt 2.1: Adds sequence numbers (0 and 1) to packets. Handles duplicate packets when ACK/NAK is garbled.
  • rdt 2.2: NAK-free protocol. Sender uses duplicate ACKs instead of explicit NAKs.
  • rdt 3.0: Channel with errors and packet loss. Adds countdown timer. Retransmits on timeout. Stop-and-Wait suffers from poor performance.

children.name: Pipelining & Sliding Window
children.details:
Pipelined Protocols

  • Sender allows multiple in-flight, unacknowledged packets.
  • Sender Utilization: {sender} = rac{N imes (L/R)}{RTT + (L/R)}$. Dramatically increases link throughput.
  • Two primary sliding window protocols: Go-Back-N and Selective Repeat.

children.name: Go-Back-N (GBN)
children.details:
Go-Back-N Protocol

  • Window size $.
  • Cumulative ACK: ACK(n) acknowledges all packets up to and including $.
  • Single timer for oldest unacknowledged packet.
  • Out-of-order packets are discarded by receiver.
  • On timeout, sender retransmits ALL $ packets in current window.

children.name: Selective Repeat (SR)
children.details:
Selective Repeat Protocol

  • Receiver acknowledges each packet individually.
  • Receiver maintains buffer for out-of-order packets.
  • Sender maintains independent timer for EACH unacknowledged packet.
  • Retransmits only the specifically unacknowledged/timed-out packet.
  • Window Size Constraint: Window size must be $\le 2^{k-1}$ (half of sequence number space) to avoid sequence number overlap ambiguity.

children.name: L9: TCP Fundamentals & Connection
children.details:
Transmission Control Protocol

RFC 793, 1122. Connection-oriented, point-to-point, full duplex, stream delivery with reliable in-order byte stream.

children.name: TCP Segment Format
children.details:
TCP Header Fields (20-60 bytes)

  • Source & Destination Ports: 16 bits each.
  • Sequence Number: 32 bits (Byte stream number of first byte in segment).
  • Acknowledgment Number: 32 bits (Next expected byte number from other side - Cumulative).
  • HLEN (Header Length): 4 bits (number of 4-byte words, 20-60 bytes).
  • Reserved: 6 bits.
  • Control Flags (6 bits): URG, ACK, PSH, RST, SYN, FIN.
  • Window Size: 16 bits (Flow control advertised receive window rwnd).
  • Checksum: 16 bits (mandatory, calculated with pseudo-header).
  • Urgent Pointer: 16 bits.

children.name: Connection Establishment (3-Way Handshake)
children.details:
Three-Way Handshake

  • Step 1 (Client->Server): SYN=1, seq=client_isn. No data payload.
  • Step 2 (Server->Client): SYN=1, ACK=1, seq=server_isn, ack=client_isn + 1. Allocates buffers.
  • Step 3 (Client->Server): ACK=1, seq=client_isn + 1, ack=server_isn + 1. Can contain data payload!
  • SYN Flood Attack: Attacker sends bogus SYNs without completing handshake; server exhausts half-open connection tables. Countermeasure: SYN Cookies.

children.name: Connection Termination
children.details:
Connection Tear-Down

  • Step 1: Client sends FIN=1, seq=u.
  • Step 2: Server sends ACK=1, ack=u + 1 (Client enters FIN_WAIT_2).
  • Step 3: Server finishes sending data, sends FIN=1, seq=w.
  • Step 4: Client sends ACK=1, ack=w + 1.
  • TIME_WAIT State: Client waits imes ext{MSL}$ (Maximum Segment Lifetime, typically 1-2 min) to allow ACK to reach server and cleanly drain stale packets from network.

children.name: L10: TCP Flow Control
children.details:
Flow Control Mechanics

Prevents a fast sender from overflowing a slow receiver buffer. End-to-end speed matching mechanism.

children.name: Sliding Window (rwnd)
children.details:
Receiver Window Dynamics

  • Receiver advertises free buffer space in Window size header: = RcvBuffer - [LastByteRcvd - LastByteRead]$.
  • Sender guarantees: - LastByteAcked \le rwnd$.
  • Window operations: Window closes (as data sent/received), shrinks (buffer reduced), and opens (as application reads bytes).
  • Zero Window Probing: When = 0$, sender sends 1-byte probe segments to trigger ACKs and discover when window reopens.

children.name: Silly Window Syndrome
children.details:
Preventing Micro-Segments

  • Problem: Either sender transmits 1-byte data or receiver advertises tiny 1-byte windows, causing massive header overhead (40 bytes header for 1 byte payload!).
  • Sender Solution (Nagle's Algorithm): Send first piece immediately; buffer subsequent data until previous ACK arrives OR full MSS accumulated.
  • Receiver Solution (Clark's Solution / Delayed ACK): Do not advertise window until \ge \min(MSS, ext{Buffer}/2)$. Delay sending ACKs up to 200ms.

children.name: L11: TCP Error & Congestion Control
children.details:
Error Recovery & Congestion Avoidance

Distinction: Flow control protects receiver buffer; Congestion control protects intermediate network routers and links.

children.name: Error Control & Retransmission
children.details:
Retransmission Triggers

  • Timeout (RTO expiration): Coarse-grained timer expires. Conservative response.
  • Fast Retransmission: Triggered on receipt of 3 duplicate ACKs (4 identical ACKs total). Sender infers lost segment and retransmits immediately without waiting for timeout!
  • Cumulative ACK generation rules: Delayed ACK (wait 200ms for 2nd segment), immediate ACK for out-of-order segment.

children.name: Congestion Control Principles (AIMD)
children.details:
AIMD Mechanism

  • Sender limits unacked data by: $\min(cwnd, rwnd)$.
  • Additive Increase: Increase $ by ext{ MSS}$ every RTT until loss occurs (probing for bandwidth).
  • Multiplicative Decrease: Cut $ in half after loss event (3 duplicate ACKs), or reset to ext{ MSS}$ on timeout.
  • Sawtooth transmission pattern achieves distributed efficiency and fairness.

children.name: TCP Tahoe vs Reno vs NewReno
children.details:
Congestion Phases

  • Slow Start: = 1 ext{ MSS}$. Doubles exponentially every RTT until \ge ssthresh$.
  • Congestion Avoidance: When \ge ssthresh$, increases linearly by ext{ MSS}/ ext{RTT}$.
  • On Loss Event:
    • Tahoe: Sets = cwnd/2$, resets = 1 ext{ MSS}$ (always enters Slow Start).
    • Reno: On 3 dup ACKs, sets = cwnd/2$, sets = ssthresh + 3 ext{ MSS}$ (Fast Recovery), skips slow start! On timeout resets = 1$.

children.name: L12: TCP RTT Estimation & Timers
children.details:
Adaptive Retransmission Timeout

Calculating dynamic RTO in a fluctuating network environment to avoid premature timeouts or sluggish recovery.

children.name: Jacobson's EWMA Algorithm
children.details:
RTT Estimation Formulas

  • EstimatedRTT (EWMA): = (1 - lpha) EstimatedRTT + lpha SampleRTT$ (typically $lpha = 0.125$).
  • DevRTT (Safety Margin): = (1 - eta) DevRTT + eta |SampleRTT - EstimatedRTT|$ (typically $ eta = 0.25$).
  • RTO Setting: = EstimatedRTT + 4 imes DevRTT$.

children.name: Karn's Algorithm
children.details:
The Ambiguity Flaw & Solution

  • Problem: When a segment is retransmitted and an ACK arrives, does the ACK belong to the 1st or 2nd transmission? Calculating SampleRTT on retransmissions severely corrupts RTO.
  • Rule 1: NEVER compute SampleRTT for any segment that has been retransmitted.
  • Rule 2 (Exponential Backoff): Whenever a timeout occurs, double the RTO: {new} = 2 imes RTO_{old}$. Backs off aggressively under network congestion.

children.name: TCP Timers Summary
children.details:
4 Core TCP Timers

  • Retransmission Timer (RTO): Tracks unacknowledged segments.
  • Persistence Timer: Prevents deadlock when receiver advertises = 0$; periodic 1-byte probes sent.
  • Keepalive Timer: Detects dead peer on idle connections (typically 2 hours).
  • TIME_WAIT (2MSL) Timer: Holds connection closed state for 2 MSL after sending final ACK.

children.name: L13: UDP (User Datagram Protocol)
children.details:
Connectionless Unreliable Transport (RFC 768)

Minimalist multiplexing/demultiplexing wrapper around IP datagrams.

children.name: UDP Characteristics
children.details:
Why Use UDP?

  • No connection establishment handshake (0 RTT startup latency).
  • No connection state (server holds no buffers, timers, or seq numbers - highly scalable).
  • Small header overhead: only 8 bytes vs 20-60 bytes for TCP.
  • No congestion control throttling: sends at constant rate dictated by application.
  • Ideal for: DNS, SNMP, DHCP, VoIP, video conferencing, online gaming.

children.name: UDP Header & Checksum
children.details:
Header & Checksum Details

  • 8-Byte Header: Source Port (16b), Destination Port (16b), Length (16b), Checksum (16b).
  • Checksum Algorithm: Treats header, payload, and a 12-byte IP pseudo-header (Source IP, Dest IP, Protocol 17, UDP Length) as 16-bit words. Computes 1's complement sum. Detects transmission bit errors.

children.name: L14: Transport Layer Security (TLS/SSL)
children.details:
Securing the Transport Layer

Providing end-to-end confidentiality, data integrity, and mutual/server authentication on top of TCP.

children.name: Security Goals & Placement
children.details:
Security Architecture

  • Confidentiality: Symmetric encryption (AES, ChaCha20) prevents eavesdropping.
  • Integrity: Message Authentication Code (HMAC / AEAD) prevents tampering.
  • Authentication: X.509 digital certificates and public key cryptography (RSA, ECDSA).
  • Placement: Implemented at the application layer above TCP (sockets wrap TLS), providing a secure socket interface.

children.name: TLS Handshake Protocol
children.details:
4-Phase Handshake

  • Phase I: ClientHello (cipher suites, nonce) & ServerHello (chosen cipher, server nonce).
  • Phase II: Server sends Certificate, ServerKeyExchange (Diffie-Hellman parameters), ServerHelloDone.
  • Phase III: Client verifies certificate, sends ClientKeyExchange (pre-master secret encrypted with server public key or DH key share).
  • Phase IV: ChangeCipherSpec & Finished messages encrypted with new session keys.
  • Key Derivation: Master secret (8 ext{ bytes}$) derived via pseudo-random function from pre-master secret + client nonce + server nonce.

children.name: TLS 1.2 vs TLS 1.3 Evolution
children.details:
Modern TLS Improvements

  • TLS 1.2 ECDHE: Requires 2 full RTTs before application data (HTTP request) can be sent. Supports legacy vulnerable ciphers (RC4, DES, CBC).
  • TLS 1.3 (RFC 8446): Reduces handshake to 1 RTT! Client sends key share in initial ClientHello. Eliminates obsolete crypto, mandates AEAD ciphers.
  • 0-RTT Resumption: Returning clients can send encrypted application data on first flight.
